column2: [The camel said:] "Revered one, by your grace let this neck of mine be long, so that it can go a full hundred yojanas to graze, lord."
[Bhishma said:] "Be it so," said the great-souled boon-giver; and obtaining that excellent boon, the camel went to his own forest.
By the boon he became slothful, that ill-minded one; the wicked, deluded by time, did not wish to graze or go.
Once, stretching out that hundred-yojana neck, he was grazing with an untired heart, when a great wind came.
Then a jackal, his limbs chilled, afflicted with hunger and weariness, with his mate quickly entered that cave, tormented by water.
Seeing it, the flesh-eating jackal, very greatly afflicted by hunger and weariness, then ate the camel's neck, bull of the Bharatas.
When that animal realised his own body being eaten, he made an effort in great pain to draw it in.
But as the animal contracted his neck up and down, by that jackal with his mate he was eaten.
Having killed and eaten the camel, the jackal then came out of the mouth of the cave when the wind and rain had passed.
Thus the camel of evil mind met his end then; see the great fault that came from the sequence of sloth.
You too, giving up this way, behave with discipline, with senses controlled; for Manu said victory has intellect for its root.
Works best done by intellect, middling by the arms, lowest by the thighs, and the least by carrying burdens, Bharata.
A kingdom stays with the able one who has gathered his senses, who guards counsel and is learned, and has good helpers, sinless one.
Aims examined stay with the doer here, Yudhishthira; with helpers the whole earth can be ruled.
This was told by the good who know the rule, in old times, of Mahendra-like splendour; I too have told it to you by the light of the scriptures; be diligent here, king."
[Bhishma said:] "On this too they recite this ancient history, the conversation of the rivers and the ocean, Bharata.
The ocean, ever the dwelling of the gods' foes, lord of rivers, asked all the rivers about a doubt that had arisen in him:

I see trees with roots and branches, shade-giving, struck down by you when you are full; but I see no reed among them.
mahabharata:12:114.5	The reed is bodiless and of little substance, and grows on your banks; was it despised, or was it not possible, or did it do something for you?
mahabharata:12:114.6	I wish to hear the opinion of all of you, how it is that these banks are broken but it is not brought under your power.
Then the river Ganga spoke a reasoned, meaningful and convincing reply to the ocean, lord of rivers:

These trees stand in their places, each having a single abode; the unwise give up that place against the current.
mahabharata:12:114.9	The reed, seeing the force coming, bows, not the others; and when the force has passed it takes its place again and stands.
mahabharata:12:114.12	One who does not bear at first the onslaught of an enemy grown great, intent on the lord's slaying and ruin, quickly perishes.
mahabharata:12:114.13	The wise man who goes about knowing the strong and weak parts of his own strength and valour and of his enemy's does not meet defeat.
mahabharata:12:114.14	So too when a learned man thinks his enemy very strong, he should take up the reed's way; this is the mark of wisdom.
[Bhishma said:] "Hear, protector of the earth, how this matter is sung: a man of ever good mind bears with one of small mind.
Not being angry at one who rages, he wins merit; the patient wipes away his own ill-doing, while the angry one grows angry again.
One should ignore him like a lapwing crying out as if in distress; fallen into the hatred of the world, he goes fruitlessly on.
Thus he is ever boasting by that sinful deed. Told this by me, one esteemed in the assembly of people stays there ashamed, withered, as if dead.
One who boasts by a deed not to be boasted of, shameless, such a lowest of men is to be ignored by the self-controlled.
Whatever the small-minded man says, one should always bear with it; for what can a vulgar man do, praising or blaming, like a senseless crow cawing uselessly in the forest?
If the evildoer's weapon were words, then words alone would be his aim; but one who wishes to kill does not aim at words.
By his conduct he displays the opposite of his origin, like a peacock dancing and as if showing his loincloth.
A man who praises in one's presence but slanders behind one's back is like a dog in the world, bound for a lost world.
Whatever such a man gives and offers, of even a hundred such people, is destroyed in an instant by slander behind the back.
Therefore a wise man should at once avoid such an evil-minded person, as the good avoid a dog's meat.
The wicked-souled man who speaks calumny against a great soul shows his own faults, like a serpent raising its hood.
One who wishes to retaliate against him who is going about his own work, unwise, is like a donkey sinking in a heap of ashes in the dust.
The unappeased wolf in the human hall, ever bent on slander of the people, like a rutting elephant trumpeting, one should abandon, like a very fierce dog.
One walking the path frequented by the unsteady, lacking restraint and humility, sinful, of hostile vows, ever wishing ill—fie on that evil-minded man.
When answered back by them, do not become distressed on hearing it; those of steady mind condemn the encounter of high with low.
Enraged, he may strike with a five-fold hand, or scatter dust or husks, or show his teeth to frighten—this is established for a fool in anger, a cruel one.
The man who bears in assembly the abuse done by a very evil man, and always recites this example, gets nothing unpleasant in speech."

This, dear one, is the sort of talk told of evil-conducted, evil-souled men; now I ask you:
mahabharata:12:116.3	What is good for the machinery of the kingdom and for the family, the rise of happiness, and what brings increase of welfare in the future and at present,
mahabharata:12:116.4	what pleases sons and grandsons, what increases the realm, what is good in food, drink and body—tell me that.
mahabharata:12:116.5	A king who is consecrated, established in the kingdom, surrounded by friends or joined with unfriendly men—how can he please his subjects?
mahabharata:12:116.6	One who takes pleasure in the support of the bad, made so by the force of affection and attachment, and from lack of mastery of his senses desires to have bad men,
mahabharata:12:116.7	all his servants, though of good family, turn to faultiness, and that king is not joined with the fruits that servants bring.
mahabharata:12:116.8	To me, standing in doubt about these royal duties so hard to find, you, equal to Brihaspati in wisdom, ought to declare them.
mahabharata:12:116.9	You, tiger among men, devoted to our family's good, are our declarer, and Kshattri the sharp-witted who always tells us.
mahabharata:12:116.12	A king without servants, alone, is not a protector; and all people of good family praise this kingdom.
mahabharata:12:116.13	For one alone cannot rule a kingdom, Bharata; without helpers, dear one, no aims can be obtained at all, and once obtained, not always guarded, bull of the Bharatas.
[Bhishma said:] "He whose whole body of servants is skilled in knowledge and science, well-wishing, of good family and affectionate, enjoys the fruit of the kingdom.
He whose ministers are of good family, not to be corrupted, who have lived with him, who give the king counsel and are skilled in knowledge of relations,
who provide for the future, expert in knowledge of time, not grieving over the past—he enjoys the fruit of the kingdom.
He whose helpers share equally his joys and sorrows, who act truly, and who think of his aims, enjoys the fruit of the kingdom.
He whose countryside, always near, is not afflicted, not mean, and relies on the good path, would share in the fruit of the kingdom.
He whose treasury register is carried by trusted, content men who increase the treasury is the best of kings.
A granary guarded by incorruptible, trusted men intent on accumulation, worthy and not greedy, would be of merit.
He in whose city the transaction shows the fruit of deeds, as written by Shankha and Likhita, would share in the fruit of dharma.
The king who has gathered men and knows kingly duty, mastering the six groups, gains fruit from dharma.

Similar to this matter is what I heard in the penance grove, what was said by the best of sages concerning Rama, son of Jamadagni.
mahabharata:12:117.3	In some great forest frequented by no men there was a sage living on roots and fruits, disciplined, with senses controlled,
mahabharata:12:117.4	devoted to initiation and restraint, tranquil, supremely devoted to study, pure, his soul cleansed by fasts, ever established in the good path.
mahabharata:12:117.5	Seeing the goodness of that wise one as he sat, all the forest-ranging creatures came near,
mahabharata:12:117.6	lions and tigers with sharabhas, rutting great elephants, leopards, rhinoceroses, bears and others of fearful look.
mahabharata:12:117.7	They all, though blood-eaters, gave him greeting, and like disciples of that sage they were submissive and obliging.
mahabharata:12:117.8	Having given greeting, they all went as they came; but one domestic animal there, a dog, did not leave the great sage.
mahabharata:12:117.9	Devoted, ever attached, weak and thin from fasting, living on piles of fruit and roots, tranquil, with the look of a good person.
mahabharata:12:117.17	Then came a very fearsome tiger, mouth gaping, hungry, licking his lips, eager for blood, toward a leopard.
mahabharata:12:117.18	Seeing the tiger, broken by hunger, fanged, a forest-ranger, the leopard took refuge in the sage to save his life.
mahabharata:12:117.19	Then the sage, ever showing the affection born of living together, turned that leopard into a tiger, stronger than his foes; and seeing him, the other tiger did not attack him, lord of men.
mahabharata:12:117.20	But the dog, having become a tiger, strong and flesh-eating, felt no longing for the enjoyment of roots and fruits.
mahabharata:12:117.21	As the lord of beasts always desires forest-dwellers, so then, great king, did that tiger.
mahabharata:12:117.22	One day the tiger, staying at the root of the hermitage, was asleep, full from slain deer, when an elephant came to that spot, risen like a rutting cloud,
mahabharata:12:117.23	with temples burst, tall, with a lotus-marked trunk, broad-headed, fine-tusked, huge of body, with a voice deep as a cloud.
mahabharata:12:117.24	Seeing that rutting elephant coming, proud with rut, the tiger, terrified of the elephant, took refuge in the sage.
mahabharata:12:117.25	Then the best of sages turned that tiger into an elephant; seeing him like a great cloud, the other elephant was afraid.
mahabharata:12:117.26	Then he wandered happily among lotus beds and thickets of shallaki trees, adorned with lotus pollen.
mahabharata:12:117.27	While the elephant was thus sporting, time passed for the sage living in his hut, night after night.
mahabharata:12:117.28	Then there came to that place a lion, reddened by his mane, born in a mountain cave, dreadful, destroyer of herds of elephants.
mahabharata:12:117.29	Seeing the lion coming, the elephant, overcome by fear of the lion, trembling with dread, took refuge in the sage.
mahabharata:12:117.30	Then the sage turned that lord of elephants into a lion; and he did not regard the wild lion, being of the same kind.
mahabharata:12:117.31	Seeing him, the wild lion fled, afraid, his strength of speech gone; and that lion lived happily in the hermitage in that same forest.
mahabharata:12:117.32	No other small animals dwelling in the penance grove were seen, terrified and ever wishing to live.
mahabharata:12:117.33	Once, by the working of time, a strong sharabha, slayer of all creatures, blood-eating, a terror of many beings,
mahabharata:12:117.34	eight-legged, with his feet raised, a forest-ranger, came to that sage's dwelling to kill the lion.
mahabharata:12:117.35	The sage made him, too, a sharabha, mighty, scourge of foes; seeing in front of him the strong, very fierce sharabha of the sage, the wild one fled quickly in fear.
mahabharata:12:117.36	Thus placed by the sage in the sharabha's place, he stayed ever at the sage's side and gained the happiness of a sharabha.
mahabharata:12:117.37	Then, terrified of the sharabha, all the herds of beasts fled from the forest in all directions, king, wishing to live.
mahabharata:12:117.38	The sharabha too, greatly corrupted, ever bent on slaughter of creatures, a flesh-eater, did not wish for a diet of peaceful fruit and roots.
mahabharata:12:117.39	Then, with thirst for blood, with strength, the sharabha wished to kill that sage, ungrateful, born of the dog's womb.
mahabharata:12:117.40	Then the sage, of great wisdom, knowing it by the power of his austerity with the eye of knowledge, said to that dog:
mahabharata:12:117.41	Dog, you became a leopard; leopard, you became a tiger; tiger, a rutting elephant; elephant, you became a lion;
lion, endowed with great strength, you again became a sharabha; out of affection I did not consider your birth and lineage.
Because, though I am sinless, you wish to kill me, sinner, therefore, returned to your own birth, you shall be a dog indeed."
Then, from his hatred of the sage, the wicked-souled sharabha, unwise, was made a dog, cursed by the sage, and regained his own form."

Thus the wise king, having learned their character and purity, honesty, nature, strength, family, conduct, learning and self-control,
mahabharata:12:118.3	compassion, strength, valour, disposition, tranquillity and forbearance, should place well-trained servants where each is fit.
mahabharata:12:118.4	A ruler is not fit to employ a servant without testing; a king crowded with men not of good family does not prosper in happiness.
mahabharata:12:118.5	One of good family employed by the king, because of that family never turns his mind to sin, even when reviled though innocent.
mahabharata:12:118.6	But a man of no family, employed by the king because of good qualities, having attained lordship hard to gain, if reproached may turn enemy.
mahabharata:12:118.7	A minister should be of good family, trained, wise, skilled in knowledge and science, knowing the truth of the meaning of all scriptures, patient and a native of the land,
mahabharata:12:118.8	grateful, strong, forbearing, self-controlled, master of his senses, not greedy, content with what he gets, wishing well to his master and friends,
mahabharata:12:118.9	knowing place and time, devoted to gathering all, honoured, steady in mind, well-wishing and untiring.
mahabharata:12:118.17	Steadfast, patient, pure, swift, knowing manly effort in due time, obedient, learned, a listener, skilled in reasoning for and against,
mahabharata:12:118.18	intelligent, retentive, acting by rule, self-controlled, ever of pleasant speech, and forbearing in adversity,
mahabharata:12:118.19	himself acting in giving and cutting off, with a good door, pleasant to behold, ever giving a hand to the afflicted, regarding himself as trusted, devoted to policy:
mahabharata:12:118.20	I am not a mere talker, nor without conflict, nor one who does anything whatever; I am the doer of deeds that are not in vain, dear to the servants."
He gathers people, is not stiff, ever of a pleasant face, a giver, looking after servants, not wrathful, greatly high-minded,
of just punishment, not without the rod, instructing in dharma's affairs, with spies for eyes, far-sighted, ever skilled in dharma and wealth.
A king filled with hundreds of virtues, so should he be sought, and warriors too, lord of men, endowed with all merits.
Good men, helpers who sustain the kingdom, should be sought out and not disrespected by a king who desires growth.
Warriors who are heroes in battle, grateful, skilled in weapons, versed in the dharma scriptures, with footmen,
grown in wealth and honour, expert in chariot-driving, skilled in bow and missiles—his is this earth, that king's.
The king who is ever intent on gathering all, diligent, rich in friends, is the best of kings.
With a thousand horses and heroic riders, Bharata, with men gathered, the whole earth can be conquered."

A dog honoured beyond measure should not be raised above his place; leaving his own place, the dog goes to another.
mahabharata:12:119.3	Wise servants of their own kind and family, established in their own works, should be employed; action in the wrong place is not fitting.
mahabharata:12:119.4	The king who gives servants works suited to them enjoys the fruit endowed with the servants' merit.
mahabharata:12:119.5	A sharabha should be set in a sharabha's place, a strong lion like a lion, a tiger like a tiger, a leopard as a leopard.
mahabharata:12:119.6	Servants should be placed by rule in fitting works; one who desires the fruit of deeds should not place his servants contrary.
mahabharata:12:119.7	A king who, exceeding measure, places servants in contrary positions is unwise and does not please his subjects.
mahabharata:12:119.8	Fools, the petty, those of uncontrolled senses and those of no family should not be placed at the side by a king who wishes his good.
mahabharata:12:119.9	Men at his side should be good, skilled, brave, learned, free from envy, not petty, pure and able.
mahabharata:12:119.10	Submissive, devoted, forbearing, clean, of natural good, they will be the king's outer agents, not reviled, each in his own place.
mahabharata:12:119.11	Beside a lion there should always be a lion; one who is not a lion, with a lion, gains the fruit like a lion.
mahabharata:12:119.12	But a lion surrounded by dogs, bent on the fruit of a lion's deed, cannot enjoy a lion's fruit when served by dogs.
mahabharata:12:119.13	Thus with these brave, wise, learned, well-born men, lord of men, the whole earth can be conquered.
mahabharata:12:119.14	Rulers of the earth should not take as a servant one without knowledge, not straight, unlearned or not very wealthy, best of those with servants.
mahabharata:12:119.15	Men devoted to their master's work go off like arrows; to the servants who are beneficial to him, king, he should apply conciliation.
mahabharata:12:119.16	The treasury should always be guarded with effort by kings; kings have the treasury as root; be a maker of the treasury's root.
mahabharata:12:119.17	Let your granary always be full, well stored with grain; let wealth and grain be entrusted to the good; be devoted to wealth and grain.
mahabharata:12:119.18	Let your servants be ever diligent and skilled in war; skill in the use of horses is wished for here.
mahabharata:12:119.19	Looking after kin and relatives, surrounded by friends and relations, seeking the welfare of the citizens' affairs, be so, delight of the Kurus.
mahabharata:12:119.20	This is your final understanding and wisdom told by me; the dog is your example, dear one. What more do you wish to hear?
The same, told in detail by former sages, seen and held by the good: tell me, bull of the Bharatas, the loving essence of the duties of kings.
[Bhishma said:] "Protection of all beings is held the highest for the kshatriya; hear, protector of the earth, how he should protect.
As the serpent-eater bears variegated plumes, so the king who knows dharma should take many kinds of forms.
Sharpness, crookedness, forbearance, truth and straightness—standing in the mean and in goodness, he thus finds happiness.
In whatever matter is beneficial, he should take on the form and colour suited to it; for a king of many forms, even a subtle aim does not fail.
His counsel should always be guarded; he should be as one mute; with fine speech and slender body, fortunate and expert in the scriptures.
He should be careful at the gates of calamity, as at places where water flows; he should take shelter in Brahmanas who are perfected, as from mountain rain-water.

A king desiring wealth should make a crest like the banner of dharma; he should always hold up the rod and act without negligence; and, seeing in the world income and expenditure, move from tree to tree.

In the rains, with his neck dark, he should sink into the lonely night; with the peacock's quality alone he should move unnoticed by women; he should not give up his armour and should guard himself by himself.
He should avoid going into the ranging grounds and snares; he should afflict that ground and again vanish in the thicket.
He should kill the angry, the very venomous, the crooked-going and the hostile; he should not shelter in a young peacock's feather; he should settle in good dwellings.
Ever like the peacock, he may do as he likes in attachment; from all sides he should take wisdom, as birds into thickets; thus, like the peacock, a king should protect his own realm.

The wise man should lay down a policy that increases himself: restraint of self by intellect, the lowering of another by intellect, and the gaining of one's own qualities by intellect—this is the instruction of the scripture.

He should reassure the other by conciliation and observe his own strength; by examining himself he should weigh intellect by intellect; the wise, intent on conciliation, should consider what to do and not to do.
The steadfast, of hidden thought, should speak when it is to be spoken; if the wise one brings up near talk, Brihaspati by his intellect would come to nature, like black iron heated in water.
The king should examine all affairs, taught by the scriptures, both his own and another's.
He should employ in their own work the petty, the cruel, the wise, the brave and the expert in wealth, and others who are superior in speech.
Even without seeing them, appointed to fitting tasks, he should follow them all, as stretched strings give their notes.
Without conflict with the dharmas he should do what is pleasing to all; the king who says "this is mine" is like an unmoving mountain.
Fixing his resolve like the sun its stretched ray, he should guard dharma alone, treating the pleasant and the unpleasant alike.
Knowing dharma, soft-spoken, from fitting family, nature and country, faultless in middle age, intent on welfare, masters of their senses,
not greedy, trained, self-controlled, firmly established in dharma—the king should place such guardians of dharma and wealth in all works.
In this way, intent, content and aided by spies, he should perform the coming and going of affairs.
For one whose anger and joy are not in vain, who himself looks into affairs and whose treasury rests on trust in himself, the earth is truly the bearer of wealth.
He whose favour is plain and whose restraint is just, whose self is guarded and kingdom guarded, is a king who knows kingly duty.
He should always look over the realm, like the sun rising with its rays; he should know the spies and the unmoving, and not be anxious by intellect.
The king should take wealth in due season and not announce it; the wise should milk the earth day by day as a cow.
As the bee gathers honey from flowers in order, so the king should take wealth and make a store.
What remains guarded is good for dharma and desire; the king who knows the scriptures and is self-possessed should store and release.
He should not despise a small aim nor slight enemies; he should know himself by intellect and not trust the unwise.
Steadiness, skill, restraint, supreme intellect, courage, valour, place and time, and carefulness—these eight kindle the growth of wealth, whether little or great.
A spark grows when fed with ghee, and a single seed becomes many thousands; seeing the great rise and fall, the wise should not despise the small."
As he was saying this, the Brahmana woman Gautami, O king, thinking that worlds depend on one's own deeds, spoke to the hunter Arjunaka.
Then he conquered all those neighbouring kings; for this reason, O king, he became famous as Karandhama.
I lie on the ground, intent on muttering, covered with kusha grass and a deerskin; and the glorious Gandhari does likewise, under the name of a vow.
Then Satyaki rose in anger and spoke, of the five sons of Draupadi, of Dhrishtadyumna and Shikhandin:
[Indra said:] "You have attained immortality, equality with me, O king, and all great fortune and great fame, and the joys of heaven today; abandon the dog; there is no cruelty in this."
Am I asleep, or awake? Am I conscious, or not? Oh, is this a disorder of my mind, or is my mind confused?
